objectives: Describe the structure and function of the cornea, aqueous humour, iris, lens, vitreous, retina, and optic nerve.
Explain phototransduction and the division of labour between rods and cones, including the role of the fovea.
Relate aqueous humour dynamics to intraocular pressure using the Goldmann equation.

slides.title: The anterior segment — cornea, aqueous, iris, and lens
slides.body:
The eye is built in two functional compartments. The **anterior segment**, from the front surface to the back of the lens, handles **refraction and light regulation**; the **posterior segment** handles **detection**. We start at the front.

The **cornea** is the transparent, avascular front window, about $0.5\,\text{mm}$ thick centrally and $11\,\text{mm}$ across. It has five classical layers: the **epithelium**, **Bowman's layer**, the **stroma** (about 90% of thickness, made of precisely spaced collagen lamellae that give transparency), **Descemet's membrane** (described by **Jean Descemet**, 1732–1810), and the **endothelium**. The single-cell endothelium runs a metabolic pump that keeps the stroma slightly dehydrated; lose those cells (as in **Fuchs' dystrophy**, named for **Ernst Fuchs**, 1851–1930) and the cornea swells and clouds. Because the cornea is avascular, it draws oxygen directly from the **tear film** and atmosphere — a fact that dominates contact-lens design.

Behind the cornea is the **anterior chamber**, filled with **aqueous humour**, a clear fluid that nourishes the avascular cornea and lens and maintains the eye's pressure and shape. Aqueous is produced by the **ciliary body**'s ciliary processes (by active secretion and ultrafiltration), flows from the **posterior chamber** through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and drains mainly through the **trabecular meshwork** into **Schlemm's canal** (after **Friedrich Schlemm**, 1795–1858), with a smaller **uveoscleral** outflow.

The **iris** is the pigmented diaphragm whose central aperture is the **pupil**. Two muscles set pupil size: the **sphincter pupillae** (parasympathetic, constricts in bright light — the **pupillary light reflex**) and the **dilator pupillae** (sympathetic, dilates in dim light or arousal). The pupil also performs an optical service: stopping it down increases **depth of focus** and reduces aberrations, the **'pinhole'** effect optometrists exploit clinically.

The **crystalline lens** sits just behind the iris, suspended by **zonular fibres** (the **zonule of Zinn**, after **Johann Gottfried Zinn**, 1727–1759) from the **ciliary muscle**. The lens is a layered, gradient-index, transparent body that supplies about $+19\,\text{D}$ unaccommodated and can add power for near vision. With age it stiffens (presbyopia) and can opacify (cataract). The lens has no blood supply and depends entirely on the aqueous for nutrition — which is why aqueous chemistry, lens metabolism, and cataract are tightly linked.

slides.title: The posterior segment — vitreous, retina, photoreceptors, and the fovea
slides.body:
Behind the lens lies the **vitreous chamber**, filled with **vitreous humour**, a clear gel of water (~99%), collagen fibrils, and **hyaluronic acid** that fills about 80% of the globe's volume and presses the retina against the wall of the eye. With age the vitreous liquefies (**syneresis**) and can separate from the retina — a **posterior vitreous detachment** — producing floaters and, occasionally, a retinal tear.

The **retina** is the neural sheet lining the back of the eye where light becomes a neural signal. It is, famously, **inverted**: light must pass through the transparent inner neural layers (ganglion cells, bipolar cells) before reaching the **photoreceptors** at the back, which abut the **retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)** and the vascular **choroid**. The microscopy of the retina was transformed by **Santiago Ramón y Cajal** (1852–1934, Nobel Prize 1906), whose drawings established its layered neuronal circuitry.

There are two photoreceptor classes. **Rods** (~120 million) are exquisitely sensitive, saturate in daylight, contain the pigment **rhodopsin**, and drive **scotopic** (night) vision; they are absent from the very centre and densest in the mid-periphery. **Cones** (~6 million) operate in bright light (**photopic** vision), mediate **colour** through three opsin types — **S (short/blue)**, **M (medium/green)**, and **L (long/red)** — and dominate the centre. The **trichromatic theory** of colour traces to **Thomas Young** (1773–1829) and **Hermann von Helmholtz**; the complementary **opponent-process theory** to **Ewald Hering** (1834–1918); both are partly correct at different stages of processing.

The **fovea** is a tiny central pit (~$1.5\,\text{mm}$) within the **macula** that contains only tightly packed cones and is responsible for sharp, detailed, **20/20** vision; its centre, the **foveola**, is so metabolically privileged that the inner retinal layers are swept aside and it is **avascular**, fed by the choroid. The **optic disc**, where ganglion-cell axons exit and retinal vessels enter, has **no photoreceptors** and is the anatomical **blind spot** mapped by **Edme Mariotte** (c. 1620–1684) in 1668.

**Phototransduction**: a photon isomerises **11-cis-retinal** to **all-trans-retinal** within rhodopsin, activating the G-protein **transducin**, which activates **phosphodiesterase**, lowering cyclic GMP and **closing** cation channels. The photoreceptor thus **hyperpolarises** to light (the reverse of most neurons), reducing glutamate release — the biochemical cascade worked out by **George Wald** (Nobel Prize 1967) and the signalling detailed by later workers. The signal then passes to **bipolar cells** and **ganglion cells**, whose axons form the optic nerve.

slides.title: Intraocular pressure and aqueous dynamics
slides.body:
The eye is a pressurised sphere, and that pressure — the **intraocular pressure (IOP)** — keeps the cornea and globe in optical shape and the retina apposed to the wall. Normal IOP averages about **15–16 mmHg**, with a population range conventionally taken as **10–21 mmHg**; it shows a **diurnal variation** (often higher in the morning) of a few mmHg. IOP is set by the balance between **aqueous production** and **aqueous outflow**, not by the vitreous or blood.

The quantitative model is the **Goldmann equation**, after **Hans Goldmann** (1899–1991), who also gave us the standard tonometer:
$$P_o = \frac{F}{C} + P_v$$
where $P_o$ is IOP (mmHg), $F$ is the **aqueous formation rate** (about $2.5\,\mu\text{L/min}$), $C$ is the **outflow facility** (the ease of drainage, about $0.2$–$0.3\,\mu\text{L/min/mmHg}$), and $P_v$ is the **episcleral venous pressure** (about $8$–$10\,\text{mmHg}$). The equation makes the pathophysiology of glaucoma transparent: pressure rises if production $F$ increases, if facility $C$ falls (a clogged or collapsed **trabecular meshwork**), or if venous pressure $P_v$ rises. Most primary open-angle glaucoma is a problem of **reduced outflow facility**.

Aqueous follows a clear circuit. The **ciliary epithelium** secretes it into the **posterior chamber**; it flows around the lens and through the pupil into the **anterior chamber**; and it leaves by two routes. The **conventional (trabecular) pathway** — meshwork → Schlemm's canal → collector channels → episcleral veins — handles roughly 80–90% and is **pressure-dependent**. The **uveoscleral pathway**, through the ciliary muscle and into the suprachoroidal space, handles the rest and is relatively pressure-independent; it is the target of **prostaglandin analogue** drops such as **latanoprost**.

Clinically, IOP is measured by **tonometry**. The gold standard is **Goldmann applanation tonometry**, which applies the **Imbert–Fick principle** ($P = F/A$, where a flat area $A$ of cornea is applanated by a known force $F$). Its accuracy depends on **central corneal thickness (CCT)**: thick corneas overestimate and thin corneas underestimate true IOP, a correction quantified after the **Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)**. Alternatives include **non-contact (air-puff) tonometry** and the rebound **iCare** tonometer. Because elevated IOP is the chief modifiable risk factor for **glaucoma**, understanding the Goldmann equation and aqueous circuit is the physiological foundation of glaucoma diagnosis and treatment — the subject of the ocular-disease lesson.

question.question: Which statement about rods and cones is correct?
options: Rods mediate colour and high-acuity central vision; cones mediate dim-light vision.
Cones are most densely packed in the fovea and mediate photopic, colour, and high-acuity vision; rods are absent from the foveola and mediate scotopic vision.
Both rods and cones are equally distributed across the retina with no regional specialisation.
Rods contain three opsin types (S, M, L) and provide trichromatic colour vision.
question.explanation: Cones are concentrated in the fovea, work in bright (photopic) light, mediate colour through the three opsins (S, M, L), and provide the high-acuity vision used for reading. Rods are far more numerous overall but are absent from the very centre (the foveola), are most dense in the mid-periphery, contain rhodopsin, and drive sensitive scotopic (night) vision. Option A reverses the two; option C ignores the strong regional specialisation; option D wrongly attributes the three cone opsins to rods (rods have a single pigment, rhodopsin).

hints: Which receptor gives you sharp daylight colour vision in the centre?
The foveola contains only one of the two receptor types.
slides.workedSolution: Cones cluster in the fovea, function in bright light, encode colour via three opsins (S/M/L), and deliver the acuity needed to read a Snellen line. Rods outnumber cones (~120 million vs ~6 million), peak in the mid-periphery, are absent from the foveola, contain rhodopsin, and serve night vision. That matches option B.

question.question: Using the Goldmann equation $P_o = F/C + P_v$, find the intraocular pressure (mmHg) for $F = 2.4\,\mu\text{L/min}$, outflow facility $C = 0.24\,\mu\text{L/min/mmHg}$, and episcleral venous pressure $P_v = 9\,\text{mmHg}$.
Aqueous humour normally follows which production-and-drainage circuit?
options: Produced by the retina, drains through the optic nerve into the cerebrospinal fluid.
Produced by the ciliary body into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil to the anterior chamber, and drains mainly via the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal.
Produced by the cornea, drains through the vitreous and choroid.
Produced by the lens, drains through the zonules into the ciliary muscle.
question.explanation: Aqueous humour is secreted by the ciliary processes of the ciliary body into the posterior chamber, passes around the lens and through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and exits chiefly by the conventional pathway: trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal → collector channels → episcleral veins (with a smaller uveoscleral route through the ciliary muscle). The retina, cornea, and lens do not produce aqueous (the cornea and lens are in fact nourished by it), so options A, C, and D are anatomically wrong. This circuit and its outflow resistance are exactly what the Goldmann equation models.

hints: The fluid is made near the lens by the ciliary body.
It drains at the angle through a meshwork into a named canal.
slides.workedSolution: The ciliary body secretes aqueous into the posterior chamber; it flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains predominantly through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal, with a minority via the uveoscleral pathway. This is option B. Reduced trabecular outflow facility is the usual lesion in primary open-angle glaucoma.

question.question: Explaining why a patient's cornea clouds after cataract surgery
question.prompt: An 82-year-old develops corneal swelling and hazy vision in the weeks after otherwise routine cataract surgery, and the surgeon notes a low endothelial cell count. Using the anatomy and physiology of the cornea — its avascular, layered structure and the role of the endothelial pump — explain why a reduced endothelial cell count leads to corneal oedema and cloudiness, why the cornea cannot simply 'heal' the lost cells the way skin does, and how this connects to the deturgescence (relative dehydration) that normally keeps the stroma transparent.

question.question: Why does each eye have a physiological blind spot, first demonstrated by Edme Mariotte in 1668?
options: Because the fovea contains only rods, which cannot resolve fine detail.
Because the optic disc, where ganglion-cell axons exit and vessels enter, contains no photoreceptors.
Because the lens casts a shadow on the central retina.
Because the vitreous gel scatters light at one fixed retinal location.
question.explanation: The optic disc (optic nerve head) is the site where retinal ganglion-cell axons converge to leave the eye as the optic nerve and where the central retinal vessels enter. It contains no rods or cones, so light falling on it cannot be detected — this is the physiological blind spot Mariotte demonstrated in 1668. The fovea is cone-rich (not rod-only) and is the point of best acuity, so option A is wrong. The lens and vitreous (options C and D) do not create a fixed non-seeing region; the blind spot is purely the absence of photoreceptors at the disc.

hints: It is located where the nerve fibres leave the eye.
No rods or cones can sit where the optic nerve exits.
slides.workedSolution: At the optic disc the ganglion-cell axons gather and exit as the optic nerve, and the central retinal artery and vein pass through; there are no photoreceptors there. Light imaged on the disc is therefore not seen, producing the physiological blind spot mapped by Mariotte in 1668. The answer is option B.
